mcqs.question: During thrashing, why can CPU utilization actually drop even though the system has more processes loaded than ever?
options: The scheduler deliberately reduces CPU speed under memory pressure
Thrashing only affects disk I/O, never CPU scheduling
Processes are constantly blocked waiting on page faults instead of running, so the CPU sits idle despite plenty of work being 'in the system'
More processes always increases utilization, so this cannot actually happen
mcqs.explanation: The CPU is idle specifically because processes are blocked on page faults, not running — more processes loaded doesn't mean more processes runnable. There's no deliberate CPU speed reduction, thrashing directly affects CPU scheduling via blocking, and this drop is exactly what defines thrashing.

mcqs.question: A system past the thrashing cliff shows low CPU utilization. Why does adding more processes make it worse instead of better?
options: Adding processes has no effect either way once thrashing has started
More processes always reduces memory pressure by spreading load evenly
Adding processes only affects disk usage, not memory
New processes take frames away from already-starved processes, increasing their fault rate and blocked time, which looks like more idle CPU and invites even more processes to be added
mcqs.explanation: Past the cliff, new processes compete for already-insufficient frames, worsening faulting for everyone and creating a feedback loop that a naive utilization-based scheduler misreads as 'add more work.' It's not neutral, doesn't spread load evenly here, and clearly does affect memory, not just disk.

mcqs.question: What's the risk of choosing a working-set window (Δ) that's too small?
options: The model wastes memory holding pages the process no longer needs
A small Δ makes the model run faster with no downside
Δ size has no effect on the working set's accuracy
The working set can undercount what a process genuinely needs, evicting pages it's about to reference again soon
mcqs.explanation: Too small a window can miss genuinely-needed pages that simply weren't referenced in the last few instructions, leading to premature eviction — the opposite risk (wasted memory) comes from too *large* a Δ. Window size clearly does affect accuracy in both directions, so neither 'no downside' nor 'no effect' is correct.

mcqs.question: How does Page-Fault Frequency (PFF) control differ fundamentally from the working set model?
options: PFF reacts to observed fault rate crossing thresholds, adjusting frames after the fact, rather than proactively modeling which pages a process needs before scheduling it
PFF and the working set model are two names for the exact same algorithm
PFF requires tracking every individual page a process has referenced
PFF only works for single-threaded processes
mcqs.explanation: PFF is reactive — it responds to fault rate after it changes — whereas the working set model proactively decides whether to schedule a process based on whether its estimated needs fit. They are different mechanisms, PFF specifically avoids per-page tracking, and neither is restricted to single-threaded processes.

mcqs.question: CPU utilization is low and page-fault rate is climbing at the same time. What's the correct response?
options: Schedule more processes to use the apparently idle CPU
Reduce the number of concurrently running processes or give existing ones more memory, since this is the thrashing signature, not spare capacity
Increase the CPU clock speed to compensate
Ignore it, since low CPU utilization always means there's room for more work
mcqs.explanation: Falling utilization plus rising fault rate together indicate thrashing, whose fix is reducing memory contention, not adding more competing processes. Adding more work, boosting clock speed, or assuming idle CPU always means spare capacity are all the wrong response to this specific signature.
